lesson.title: Algorithms: Step-by-Step Problem Solving
lesson.summary: This section explains what an algorithm is in cognitive psychology, why following one guarantees a correct solution, and when that guarantee comes at the cost of speed.
lesson.body:
You already know that psychology insists on systematic, testable methods rather than guesswork ,  an algorithm is that same commitment to system applied inside your own thinking. An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure that, if followed correctly and completely, is guaranteed to produce a correct solution to a problem. The key word is guaranteed: an algorithm doesn't rely on hunches, shortcuts, or prior experience with similar problems. It works because it methodically considers every relevant possibility or applies a fixed rule in the same way every single time, leaving no room for a correct answer to slip through unconsidered.

Think about a three-digit combination lock. The digits run from 0 to 9 in each of three positions, so there are 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000 possible combinations. If you forgot the code but were determined to open the lock without any hints, an algorithmic approach would be to start at 000 and try every combination in order ,  000, 001, 002, and so on ,  until the lock opens. This is tedious, and in the worst case you'd need all 1,000 attempts, but it cannot fail. Because the procedure systematically covers the entire space of possibilities, success is mathematically certain as long as you carry it out completely. That certainty is the defining feature of an algorithm: the method itself, not luck or insight, is what produces the answer.

Algorithms show up constantly in ordinary cognition, not just in locks and math homework. The procedure you learned for long division is an algorithm ,  apply the same sequence of divide, multiply, subtract, and bring down, and you will always land on the correct quotient. Following a recipe exactly, step by step, is another example: if you measure and combine ingredients in the specified order and amounts, you'll reliably get the same dish. Computer programs are built almost entirely out of algorithms, which is part of why psychologists borrowed the term when they began comparing human thinking to information processing.

The tradeoff is time and effort. Notice that in the lock example, you might get lucky and hit the right combination on your third try, but you might also need all 1,000 ,  the algorithm doesn't know which, so it keeps grinding through the full sequence unless it happens to hit the answer early. For a problem with only a handful of possibilities, that cost is trivial. But for problems with enormous numbers of possible solutions ,  imagine trying to find one specific word by testing every possible letter combination ,  an exhaustive, guaranteed-correct approach can become so slow that it's impractical even though it would technically work eventually.

Understanding algorithms matters for a psychological reason beyond math or coding: it sets up a contrast you'll need for later material on how people actually solve most everyday problems. Because true algorithms are often slow, effortful, or simply unavailable for messy real-world decisions, human cognition frequently trades that guarantee of correctness for speed instead. Keeping clear on what an algorithm is ,  a complete, rule-governed procedure that always works if followed fully ,  gives you the baseline against which those faster, less certain strategies will later be measured.
